en: Twenty diversions have been fully described by King Soma;
now, the most enchanting mountain-game shall be told.
There, one should construct a forest on all sides filled with various trees; in its center, for the sake of recreation, there should be a beautiful, charming, and captivating grove.
The king should cause a mountain to be constructed, resplendent with lofty peaks,
filled with various trees, and possessing vast, level plateaus.
There, the trees with variegated fruits were fashioned by that very application.
Those who had other wives and other sons were protected by him like his own children.
Abounding in infinite fruit, endowed with fruit at all times, even those that are small become large-bodied; those that have become crooked are praised.
On the mountain, various fruit-bearing trees, endowed with other sweet fruits that yield their produce at the very moment they are desired, have been planted with great effort.
Having ripened naturally, it becomes free from defects;
having dried it in the sun, one should smear the seed and fruit with cow dung for five days.
One should fumigate [the seeds] thoroughly with the incense of *viḍaṅga* and ghee;
this is recorded as the procedure for the seeds of all trees.
The seed, soaked in cow's milk continuously for ten nights and dried in the shade,
is then combined with the milk of vyāghrī and with ashes.
Having mixed barley and wheat with cow dung and smeared [the ground], one should place it under milk-trees; this is the ritual preparation of the seed.
In a region with sweet-tasting water, free from anthills and stones,
rich in fertile soil, moist, and devoid of frost;
Having sown sesame seeds as well as mung beans, and seeing the grove abounding in flowers and fruits,
one should construct a pleasure-grove all around that pleasure-mountain.
The distance between trees being planted should be sixteen, eleven, eight, or likewise fourteen cubits.
Having understood the large, medium, and small [measures] according to their application,
this distinction of intermediate sizes has been declared by those skilled in the science of meters.
Having dug a pit measuring four cubits in depth and the same in width,
and having filled it with abundant bones and dried cow-dung, one should burn it intensely.
Then, having removed the ashes, one should fill it with sand or clay;
one should perform a sprinkling of goat-flesh and fat with water mixed with those substances.
When seeds are sown there, beautiful trees grow;
or else, those which are brought from elsewhere are planted along with their very roots.
The Aśoka, Nimba, Punnāga, Bakula, Nāgakeśara,
Śirīṣa, and Tilaka trees are likewise planted first in the grove for the increase of happiness,
health, fame, fortune, and victory.
For the sake of good fortune, these trees should be planted by the king in the forest.
The palāśa, the kāñcanāra, the ciñcā, the śleṣmātaka, the arjuna,
and the karañja— these trees should not be planted in a grove by one who desires happiness.
In the winter and the cool season, water should be given at intervals during the day;
likewise, in the spring and the summer, it should always be given in the morning by the wise.
During the rainy season and in the autumn, when the surface of the earth has become dry,
water should then be poured by those who know the proper way into the basins around trees.
When the water remaining in a reservoir does not undergo drying up, one should know that it is undigested; such water should not be given [as a purgative].
Having dug the ground in that manner and allowed the standing water to dry up,
one who desires the growth of trees should subsequently perform the watering.
From frost, from intense heat, from smoke, and likewise from fire,
trees must be protected with great effort from the spider's web.
One who desires the growth of trees must carefully uproot all grass, shrubs, creepers, and the like that have grown nearby, along with their very roots.
Taking earth from a tree burnt by lightning in the Nandana grove, she should scatter it over them for their protection; by that means, they will not suffer from the cold.
In the forest, white śāli rice mixed with curd and rock salt should be thrown upon the surface of the earth to ward off the rain of hailstones.
A wise person should prepare an incense using nightshade, viḍaṅga, white mustard, flowers from the arjuna tree, and the flesh of the catfish and the rohita fish.
This incense of fruits and flowers produces abundant prosperity;
it quickly wards off wood-boring insects and destroys the diseases of trees.
Viḍaṅga, hiṅgu, rock salt (sindhūttha), black pepper,
ativiṣā, vacā, bhallātaka, and buffalo horn, taken in equal parts.
Yoga endowed with these [mantras] shall destroy worms and insects;
when applied to trees in a garden, it is the destroyer of all diseases.
Beginning from the sowing of the seeds, one should water with a single jar until the year is complete;
thereafter, one should increase the number of jars by one each year.
Then, by that same measure, water should be diligently given to the trees at the proper time, twenty times for each [unit].
Provided with the fruits of all seasons and always adorned with fruit,
it was fashioned from shapharī, ghee, white mustard, and plantain leaves.
Incense makes the place of trees glossy and productive of fruit;
likewise, ghee and honey mixed with water boiled from *aṅkola* is effective.
The trees, sprinkled with the fat of the kirikuraṅga deer,
are endowed with fruits of all seasons and are always adorned with fruit.
In the Nandana grove, trees laden with leaves, flowers, and fruits are seen,
having been watered with viḍaṅga, honey, clarified butter, and milk.
Milk-trees fumigated with *nata*, *jatu*, and *kuṣṭha* always bear fruit;
likewise, [trees] treated with water boiled with *kuṣṭha*, cow's milk, and fat [bear fruit].
The creepers sprinkled with goat's gall, water boiled with kuṣṭha, cow's milk, and fat shall always bear fruit.
The creepers of the *aja-gara* tree, when sprinkled with [the aforementioned mixture], will bear fruit at all times;
likewise, the *vṛścika-ākara* trees, when fumigated with cow’s ghee, [will yield fruit].
Creeper-vines sprinkled with the fat of a rat and the bile of a lizard always bear fruit;
likewise, when the flesh of a fish and its broth are poured upon a cock's dung, [the same result follows].
The grape becomes very sweet and adorned with abundant fruit through [the influence of] Sāraṅga,
Gaja, Mārjāra, Krodha, Cāpa, and Phaṣapa.
A pomegranate tree, sprinkled with fat and milk, yields sweet and excellent fruit;
likewise, for anyone, the flesh of a cow mixed with cow's milk and jaggery [yields such fruit].
When the roots have been sprinkled with that, the orange tree will become abundant in fruit.
Water boiled with *aṅkola* and the fat of a honey-bear (*madhukroḍa*) [should be used].
By that [water], mango trees watered at their roots shall always bear fruit;
having performed the act of wrapping [the seed] with the husk (palāla) of a lotus, [it should be sown].
The jackfruit should be eaten with its hairs bristling with joy,
mixed with honey, clarified butter, jaggery, milk, and meat broth.
The kapittha and śrīdruma trees, which were endowed with abundant and sweet fruit,
were sprinkled [with water] after the Kumāra had first inflicted a wound upon them at the time of their flowering.
The site of the wound was smeared with a paste made from the powder of *japā* (or *payā*) and sesame seeds, mixed with honey and ghee, so that it took on the appearance of mud.
The āmalakī tree produces many sweet fruits when pierced by a heated needle inserted with the excrement of a boar or a horse.

In the section on the description of fruit essences (*phalagarbha*), *rambhā* becomes *bhūtiriphala*. [One should prepare it] with *viḍaṅga*, black gram, *madhuka*, and *surā*, all kept cool with jasmine flowers.
One who applies an ointment made from powdered *madirā* mixed with blood and combined with salt will, during the night,
always be free from [the loss of] semen.
The coconut tree produces a large fruit that is very sweet;
[this is prepared] with equal parts of the powder of sesame, honey, and liquorice.
When all the roots of the jujube tree (*badarī*) are sprinkled with a mixture of honey and water from the *kusumajananī* plant,
it bears fruit instantly.
With a golden probe, she [applied] sweet, fragrant, and large fruits that were like the powder from the tusks of lordly elephants.
If a plantain tree is pierced at its base with a fruit or root, it will produce large fruits;
likewise, [a similar effect occurs with] a *bhoḍī* made from ivory or one produced from the tusks of a boar.
When the trunk-juice of a stinking elephant is applied to the bulbous root of a plantain tree and firmly covered with earth,
it causes the plantain to grow exceedingly.
One should offer a collection of fruits held in a vessel made from the tusks of a lordly elephant,
along with oil-cake, liquor, seeds, fish, mice, and meat.
A citron tree with large fruit that has been sprinkled with water consecrated by a perfected one (siddha),
or a royal jambu tree whose leaves have been sprinkled with a decoction of śīra and mustā, [becomes effective].
The mango tree may also be called *sahakāra*, and the *sahakāra* is exceedingly fragrant;
yet it is [rendered foul] by the fat from the eyes of horses, elephants, deer, jackals, and oxen.
An *āmra* tree, when sprinkled with boiled milk and water from the five shoots (*pañcapallava*),
becomes a fragrant *sahakāra*.
This very same formulation, when combined with liquorice (mura),
produces an excellent fragrance for all varieties of flowers.
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by swarms of humming bees as they [passed over] the kubja,
śoṇita, nāga, punnāga, and kesara trees.
One should fashion trees endowed with blossoming growth and enchanting with fragrance;
[trees] struck by the foot-strikes of a young woman adorned with anklets.
The *aśoka* tree quickly blossoms with its filaments due to the impact of her face;
the *tilaka* tree is struck by her eye, which is reddened by intoxication.
The Punnāga and Nāgacampaka trees are adorned with the ear-ornaments of lovely women; the Tilaka tree is covered by the pollen from the sandalwood paste on the breasts of beautiful women.
Adorned with the auspicious rites of the marriage ceremony and joined by the ritual of union, she provides a flowery livelihood through drops of nectar.
A *śyāmā* creeper near a nearby tree will not bear flowers;
likewise, at the end of the day, *karavīra* and *kuraṇṭaka* plants do not possess wine.
The mādhavī vines bear charming blossoms at all times;
yet the mallikā, timid against the cold, is scorched by the fire of straw.
It produces flowers in abundance during the cold season and is frequented by swarms of bees;
when its root is sprinkled with milk, the japā flower becomes crimson.
The karṇikāra, japā, aśoka, bāṇa, and āmrātaka trees produce white flowers that shine like the rays of the moon.
By means of this yoga, they produce white flowers in the Nandana grove;
and all those [flowers], being permeated by the fragrance of blossoms, are as if filled with raw nectar.
When Saturn and Mars are cast upon the asterism of the "outpouring of flowers" (Puṣya),
one should sprinkle trees with abundant scented water once every day.
Within just one month, they produce fragrance even from a flower devoid of scent,
provided it has been perfumed with the aroma of any flower whatsoever.
One should pour a large quantity of clay and fragments from the roots of trees,
along with the powders of *gandha*, *patra*, *surā*, *mustā*, *tagara*, and *uśīra*.
How could fragrance arise from that [reed] when it is merely mixed with water?
[Yet] when it is smeared with honey and clarified butter in its youth and childhood, and wrapped with thread—
Having united, they produce a cluster of cool and red blossoms;
the creeper, anointed with honey, bears flowers that are intensely red.
Anointed with clarified butter, it produces beautiful white flowers;
likewise, the roots of the kumuda and ambhoja lilies [produce them] when treated with honey and clarified butter.
From two [vessels] filled with the powder and paste of *kalāya*,
two auspicious flowers arise from a single stalk alone.
The white water-lily and the lotus indeed cause wonder in the lake;
by means of realgar and yellow orpiment, the state of a water-boar [is produced].
A Campaka tree sprinkled with milk will produce saffron blossoms when treated with a mixture of liquorice (yaṣṭī),
horse gram (kūlattha) powder, and honey.
The root of *madhūka* that has the color of heated [metal] should be sprinkled with water at its base;
it should then be infused for seven days with human flesh and *saṅkolla* oil.
A seed sown in the soil of a human skull sprouts immediately when sprinkled twenty-one times with the blood of a cock.
At that very moment, a pomegranate seed certainly grows and bears fruit when it has been thoroughly saturated with the fat of fish,
boar, or goat, along with milk.
The seed of any tree whatsoever may quickly produce flowers and fruit;
for instance, the seed of a ripe mango tree, when sown, [yields results] within seven days.
Then, by constantly mixing the ashes of the *bṛhatī* plant and sesame stalks with fish, boar, fat, oil, ghee, and milk,
and sowing [the seed] therein, it grows immediately; it becomes flowering and even bears fruit.
With human flesh, fat, blood, and the powdered tusks of elephants.
A plantain tree sprinkled with water mixed [with these] will bear fruits of pride;
likewise, an aṅkolla tree [will bear fruit] when sprinkled with a decoction of jujube, blood, and fat.
A plantain tree,
when sprinkled with [the juice of] liquorice flowers and white kuṣṭha mixed with honey, produces excellent pomegranate fruit.
Having made a paste of *niṣpāva* and *aṅguli*, and having extracted the root,
the wise man should apply this procedure to whichever tree he intends to treat.
Its fruit becomes seedless and exceedingly sweet;
dog's meat, boiled in a decoction of *aṅkolla* and mixed with goat's milk, [is likewise transformed].
One should place oil-cake at the root of a mango tree;
thus the mango tree will become like a grapevine, bearing fruit at all times.
It is certain that a wondrous thing has been given into the hearts of all:
the branch of the tree has borne fruit, encircled by seven coils.
At the junction of Kṛṣṇa’s ploughshare,
she was firmly bound with such a bond made of the hide grown from his neck.
It yields green fruit at all times without being cooked;
its branch is bound with skin and fastened to the neck of a goat.
One should take an unripe fruit from any tree whatsoever and place inside it honey and ghee mixed with young cucumber.
At the end of a fortnight, one should carefully extract the seeds of the eggplant (*vārtāka*);
when sown, they will produce a creeper covered with pumpkin leaves.
There, fruits are produced— this is truly marvelous—
consisting of eggplants made from the powders of barley, black gram, sesame, and rice, combined with minced meat.
Watered with water mixed with tamarind and thoroughly fumigated at night,
this plant exists in the form of a creeper, abounding in fruits that are pleasant and sweet to the taste.
This wonderful account of the trees there has been related according to their application;
such is the interior of this forest, made beautiful by its mountains.
He fashioned artificial trees, lakes, and likewise rivers,
with leaves made of green cloth and flowers made of gold.
There were vast trees with silver branches and fruits fashioned from coral,
providing cool shade and crafted with many artistic designs.
[He saw] clusters of fragrant flowers accompanied by fruits as sweet as nectar;
[he saw] a vessel filled with pure water, adorned with swans and other birds fashioned from conch shells;
and [he saw] it strewn with cucumbers and plantains, along with shimmering golden lotuses.
On the mountain, one should construct a lake with a new platform made of sapphires, adorned with excellent elephants, and having the appearance of a mirror for the women of the quarters.
In some places, one should cause small channels to be made, filled with saffron water and featuring sandy banks fashioned from fine pearls.
Having thus constructed such a mountain, he was then filled with intense joy; accompanied by his beloved wives and surrounded by those who had attained wealth through his favor, he remained there.
Having summoned men who were kings, as well as learned and highly discerning scholars, the protector of the earth, adorned with the splendor of his finery, [addressed them].
Having mounted an excellent steed, adorned with playful ornaments,
beautiful as if speaking with the sounds of golden tinkling bells.
Shaded by a white lotus and fanned with white yak-tail whisks,
he was glorious like Purandara, surrounded by the gods.
Attended by women as delightful as celestial nymphs,
he should proceed slowly and comfortably until he reaches the edge of the forest and enters it.
Pointing out to the fawn-eyed women trees that bring delight to the eyes, yet which also produce delusion— even though they were perfectly circular— Caitra [acted].
Then Raghava ascended that mountain-like Puṣpaka chariot,
stretching out his long arm which resembled the branch of a celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
Having forcibly seized the fortune of rival kings through his valor,
the king would drag away their young women and cause them to be placed upon that mountain.
And he should cause his retinue and those who have arrived from foreign lands to mount [the vehicle] with affectionate words, preceded by great respect.
Abounding in coral fruits, endowed with petals like the silken garments of Hari,
magnificent with golden flowers, and resplendent with jewel-like wings.
There were artificial trees that rivaled the Kalpavṛkṣa,
and a lake filled with water, resplendent with golden mud.
Campāśrī was made muddy with powdered sandalwood and strewn with jewel-sand; it was provided with moonstone slabs and flowing streams of saffron water.
The king should display his army, which captivates the eyes and mind,
as well as his retinue of women whose eyes are like the petals of blue lotuses.
There, amorous women sport, graced by the gait of swans,
their pairs of breasts beautiful like wheels, and their faces like blooming lotuses.
Having sat down at the foot of a tree of variegated jewels upon a crystal stone pedestal, the lord of the earth partook of many divine fruits of precious gems.
One should give golden and saffron-colored flowers, as well as divine garments for petals,
to those worthy of favor and also to the one who has attained the perfect circle.
Then, having dismissed them all, the lord of the earth, surrounded by beautiful women, shone like Śakra amidst the hosts of Apsarases.
In some places under the shade of trees, in some places on the banks of rivers,
and in some places on the shores of lakes, the lord of the earth sports.
One should have sweet-voiced birds sing and cause graceful women to dance;
by making a group of young women laugh, one shall attain supreme bliss.
Having gathered beautiful flowers that have been perfumed with other scents,
one should present them to young women for the sake of adornment.
Then, having descended from the mountain peak and mounted his excellent elephant,
the illustrious one should proceed to his own city, resplendent with divine musical instruments.
Thus has this mountain-climbing sport, which excites the curiosity of men,
been described by Bhūlokamalla Deva, whose fame is renowned.
(Thus ends the sport on the mountain.
1) Now, the delightful forest sport is described in detail:
once the cold season has passed, the king should engage in sports centered in the forest.
When the spring season had arrived, with the southern Malaya breeze blowing—
cool, pleasant to the touch, and enchanting with the fragrance of flowers.
When the wind, reddened by the pollen of nāgakesara, punnāga, mango, and campaka flowers,
delighted the faces of the women who were the quarters of the sky.
While the song of beloved companions was harmonious, while the weeping of followers had ceased,
and while the cry of the cuckoo brought joy to the hearts of young women;
When the multitude of mango trees was in bloom, when the campaka trees were in full flower,
and when the *bakula* and *kesara* trees were beautiful with blossoms and richly adorned with flowers.
Fragrant with the scent of *jambīra* and *sumana* flowers, intense with the blossoms of *pāṭalā*, and beautified by blooming *mucukunda* clusters and the splendor of abundant, fragrant blue lotuses;
It was beautified by *karṇikāra* trees with the luster of gold, by red *aśoka* trees that were intensely radiant,
by clusters of white *mādhavī* blossoms, and likewise by creepers and *campaka* trees.
It was filled with dense, auspicious *kramuka* and *bhavya* trees standing in rows,
along with beautiful *sarala* trees and enchanting coconut palms laden with fruit as heavy as clouds.
With orange trees rich with fruits the color of vermilion-red,
and with tall trees whose fruits resemble well-rounded breasts;
"With a single fruit we shall bring satisfaction to the worlds"—
as if with these words, the jackfruit trees stood with their horripilation manifest like bristling thorns.
The interior of the forest was adorned with excellent plantain groves that shielded against the sun’s heat,
and with rows of trees beautified by clusters of fruit.
It was adorned with nīpa, nīvāra, jambīra, and jambu trees,
as well as kapittha, lakuca, āmra, and prācīnāmalaka trees.
With pomegranate trees, citron trees, and young clove trees;
with sidhrīkā, tāla, hintāla, tilaka, and sarala trees.
With groves of date palms and ketakī flowers, with branches of mallikā jasmine,
and with fragrant tagara, śatapatra, and karavīraka blossoms.
With pigments of the color of water-lilies, with yellow and black kuraṇṭaka flowers,
and with turmeric, ginger, sāraṇa, and karikarṇaka plants.
It was resplendent here and there with *damanaka* and *maruka* flowers,
and adorned with vine-arbors of grapes rich with long-hanging clusters of blossoms.
It was covered with excellent *karañja* trees thick with abundant fruit,
dense with *kṣīrika* trees, and shaded by thickets of *tāla* palms.
In a forest where the ground was cool, fragrant, and swept clean,
delightful with flowing streams and provided with two openings of sand.
In a pleasure grove, the king may sport with mental delight derived from various sights, free from hunger and thirst, and possessing a splendor that rivals the Nandana garden.
With eyes like blue lotuses, rows of teeth like pomegranate blossoms,
necks like the trunks of betel-nut trees, and arms as soft as śirīṣa flowers.
With creeper-like slender bodies, they sported with hands as straight and long as *sarala* trees, shimmering with *kaṅkeli* sprouts,
and with fingernails like *ketakī* flowers.
He was surrounded by beloved women, who were charming with the melodious warbling of cuckoos, the eloquent speech of parrots, and the graceful gait of swans.
With breasts resembling *kapittha* fruits and names that were well-known,
they were other recipients of his favor, accustomed to the pleasures of jesting.
Accompanied by jesters, servants, and buffoons skilled in the entertainment of song and instrumental music,
the lord of the earth should mount either horses or female elephants.
For the sake of sport, he may go to the forest like another Purandara;
having warded off the people, he himself shall enter at the very front.
He should show his beloveds delightful regions of various colors;
he should resort to cool shade while remaining upon pleasant grounds.
Bending the branches of trees and gathering the fruit held within them,
he plucked fragrant flowers and tender shoots.
Wandering here and there, the king was surrounded on all sides by beautiful women who,
in that dense thicket, concealed their own forms.
Having become concealed by the young shoots, he deceives the glances of his beloved;
the beloveds run here and there, desiring to see him.
Filled with love, they embraced the king as soon as they saw him;
and having done so for him in that manner, they brought him exceeding joy.
They fled before the king, and the king likewise [fled] before them;
they were slightly overcome by fatigue, [refreshed] by the cool water of the channels.
Having washed his face and feet,
the lovely women, who increase desire, fanned the king with fans made of plantain leaves.
Then the king, together with his attendants, sat down, taking recourse in the cool shade in delightful regions.
Having tasted various fruits that are like nectar,
one should drink the divine, cool, and pure water of the coconut.
Then, having caused them all to drink, one should attain supreme joy;
and having brought betel nuts and betel leaves, [one should proceed].
One should give them what is appropriate and then personally taste [the offering] with the resin of sandalwood trees mixed with camphor powder.
One should smear all the limbs with unguents and likewise anoint one's own body;
and [one should offer] fragrant flowers strung together by women.
The charming king himself should place flowers upon the *khompaka* for his beloved women as an offering of love.
Then she should prepare a cluster of flowers to delight the heart of her beloved;
thereafter, when a portion of the day remains, she should depart from her own residence.
"A protector of the earth might come, appearing like a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
Thus was this forest sport described by King Soma.
Always bestowing joy upon kings and kindling their passion—
[thus ends the forest sport]. Now, the sport of swinging, which is dear to the heart, shall be described.
When the king of seasons, the exceedingly enchanting spring— the supreme ally of Kandarpa in his affliction of throngs of amorous women— had fully arrived.
One should perform the ritual movement (āndolana) using a structure provided with two large pillars;
one should place four pillars on each side of those two pillars.
On all sides of the two pillars, beautiful and variegated figurines should be fashioned;
and then one should place pavilions and dwellings above them.
One should firmly fasten three silk cloths upon those pillars;
above them, a beautiful [canopy] fashioned in successive tiers should be made.
It was endowed with fifteen peaks, draped in garments of various colors,
and exceedingly beautiful with trees in the form of deities and lovely creepers.
Adorned with peacocks, elephants, swans, lions, tigers, and monkeys,
that beautiful and radiant array of various forms was fashioned.
Having fashioned it thus, one should thoroughly and properly apply it with powders;
then, one should fix it very firmly upon the back of the wooden board.
Beautiful wooden chains, auspicious and inlaid with gold, should be made in great numbers, all equal in length, and suspended around [the stūpa].
On the lower surface of the band, in the middle portion,
one should fashion a bud with many petals, known as the "inner golden" (sauvarṇāntara).
It was pinned with a wedge, firmly secured so as not to wobble,
bound with four leather thongs, and joined by a wooden plank.
It was yoked to rutting elephants, covered in gold,
square-shaped, delightful, radiant, and captivating to the mind.
Thus the swing was prepared at the arrival of night on the full moon;
then the king, adorned with jewels and full of passion, appeared as the moon rose.
Accompanied by women, like Śakra with hosts of Apsarases,
he was honored by a great sound of musical instruments and by a multitude of bards.
Accompanied by the entertainment of song and instrumental music and praised by Brahmins who partake of food,
he should then ascend the swing together with his beloved wives.
Then, being praised by the people with their palms joined in reverence amidst shouts of "Victory! Victory!", the king shone like the King of the Gods.
Having gratified the Brahmins, the singers, and all others with pleasant words, gold, garments, and ornaments, he should then dismiss them all.
Then the king, filled with joy, sported with his beloved women on swings amidst the moonlight,
which was as white as powdered sandalwood.
In the center of the seat, the king himself should remain comfortably seated with his beloved,
his long arms resembling the trunk of an elephant in rut.
His body pressed by the breasts of the slender-limbed woman on either side,
he was clad in the armor of horripilation born of the joy of their embrace.
With her two arms bound by a rope around his body from front to back,
she stands upright, having firmly pressed her buttocks against his private parts.
They displayed their slender waists, as well as their rounded breasts,
their smooth armpits, and their beautiful pair of plantain-stalk-like thighs.
Thus increasing passion like the moonlight does the ocean,
she likewise caused the swing to rock here and there with the strokes of her feet.
With the waves of his intellect utterly agitated like an elephant watched by hunters,
his limbs drenched in sprays of pleasure, and his flesh transformed by joy,
four beautiful women stationed in the four directions should sing.
Accompanied by sweet and melodious songs that rival the warbling of the cuckoo and resound with the roar of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
Swinging it slowly, slow, with the king's name inscribed upon it,
the two slender-limbed women, by their swaying, captivated the mind of the monarch.
Though endowed with beauty and youth, they drew him in as if by their melodious voices;
under the pretext of rolling a wooden board with their feet, they provoked his envy.
When the king, looking back with longing at his beloveds, was thus agitated by anger,
this sport of swinging was described by King Somamahībhujā.
[Thus ends the game of swinging.
3] Now he will describe that very same game of sprinkling (*secanakrīḍā*) according to its characteristics and definitions,
during the festival of spring or at festivals such as weddings and the like.
Or, having won, the king, filled with joy, may engage in sexual play;
the king, having finished his meal, does so when two watches of the night have passed.
The protector of the earth, preceded by his doorkeepers, summoned the princes,
the lords of the provinces, the vassals, and many others.
Likewise, he should appoint a family priest, as well as wise counselors, ministers, and secretaries—
valiant warriors endowed with political wisdom and experts in the duties of service.
[He appointed] those who knew the mind, ministers of Dharma, wealthy men of great fortune,
poets, those skilled in the arts, and likewise eloquent disputants.
[He summoned] reciters, those skilled in song, experts in dance, instrumental music, and the like,
as well as heralds, wandering bards, and panegyrists such as the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins.
Others, with minds full of serene faith, were adorned in white garments;
some were endowed with various ornaments, while others were beautified by garlands of flowers.
One should have those who are adorned with sandalwood tilakas enter the very spacious pavilion and seat them there for a short while, as is appropriate.
Then there were the courtesans of the city, who were as if the very embodiments of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
as well as the women of the inner apartments and the ladies of the harem.
There were slender-limbed young women with full, rounded breasts,
lovely with faces like the full moon, dark-complexioned and possessing beautiful eyes.
Delighting in a gait like that of a swan, their locks of hair surpassed bees in beauty;
sweet with voices as melodious as the song of the cuckoo, they possessed hair as dark as a rain cloud.
Their arms were like lotus stalks, their feet resembled red lotuses,
they wore white jackets, and they were not excessively adorned with gold.
They were enriched with golden lotuses, adorned with golden ketaka flowers,
marked with golden swans, and beautified by golden earrings.
There were necklaces of camphor and pearls, as well as chains and sacred threads,
all beautifully adorned with crests shining like refined gold.
Their feet were adorned with bracelets, anklets, and small bells,
and they were captivating with magnificent golden girdles of exquisite design.
Clad in white garments and beautifully anointed with saffron,
were they celestial nymphs descended to the world of mortals, or perhaps external personifications of Rati?
Are they perhaps the mental fluctuations of men personified as embodied forms?
Or are they the presiding deities of passion, the very mothers of the erotic sentiment?
Reflecting thus, they all entered the king's palace,
having approached the monarch with their faces upturned, intent upon beholding his countenance.
The king sportively sat down with those women who were like moonlight upon an ocean of joy,
as well as with golden-shouldered men and vast reservoirs of water.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water mixed with powdered saffron,
combined with sandalwood paste, and blended with musk-paste.
With flowers endowed with the fragrance of camphor and mixed with various types of agallochum,
as well as with mallikā, mādhavī, utpala, and kamala flowers.
With *pāṭala* and *śatapatra* flowers, fragrant *karavīra* blossoms,
and with cool waters covered by garments gathered into bundles, [he honored] them.
The king should cause those standing in rows to hold their elbows full;
[he should provide] horns made of gold and silver, as well as horns of the gayal.
And he should place various mechanical devices that discharge streams of water,
as well as golden pitchers, into the hands of the women.
Clad in bright garments, perfumed with camphor and agallochum,
adorned with jasmine wreaths upon their heads, and decorated with the moon and stars.
Is he Madana endowed with limbs, or is it Spring incarnate? Or is he the presiding deity of the festival, or perhaps the very abode of the erotic sentiment?
Thus being thus exhorted, the king would then rise up,
surrounded by a limited number of people amidst the great sound of musical instruments.
The lord of the earth should come with water for the elbows,
having filled the horns, the water-machines, and the jars with water.
Beloved women, their minds filled with joy,
sprinkle the king with those waters reddened by saffron and with waters white as sandalwood paste.
A king should sprinkle his servants with waters darkened by musk and with forests turned tawny by turmeric, like the rain-god Parjanya incarnate.
Like another Indra, he should joyfully delight the worlds with nectars;
filled with gladness, he should scatter flowers upon their heads.
The king of noble conduct shines like a wish-fulfilling tree,
with soft balls made of silk thread and perfectly round.
If beloved women strike with playful charm, like the risen god whose weapon is flowers,
they cause even the hard heart to melt away, as if washing it clean.
One should sprinkle the assembly of young women so that the creeper of love may flourish;
one woman embraces her beloved, while another draws his hand toward her.
One woman grasps the hem of his garment, another takes hold of his turban;
thus the king is thrown into utter confusion by them on all sides.
With his body bristling with horripilation from the joy of the excellence of his good fortune,
that king thus performed the sport of service with ease.
Then, when the sun had grown dim, the king desisted from his sport;
casting off his wet garments, he put on fine robes.
The king, enriched by the splendor of his jewel-ornaments, should sit upon the lion-throne;
[he should also provide] garments, gold, jewels, and various ornaments individually.
Having given [gifts] according to their merit and joined with mental respect, one should dismiss them all;
thus has the practice of service and sport been described by King Soma.
[Thus ends the game of courtship. Now, the exceedingly enchanting game of water-play is described. This [game] is eternally pleasing to kings who utterly destroy hosts of enemies.
When the summer heat had arrived and the orb of the sun was fierce,
the people of the world were tormented and afflicted by the thirst and exhaustion resulting from their longing for coolness.
In a forest devoid of leaves, upon the surface of the earth intensely scorched by heat,
where the ground was agitated by mirages mingled with hot winds.
In that parched lake, where the water has completely dried up and long whirlpools of dust are spinning, scorched by the forest fire born from the friction of bamboo and dry wood;
The lord of the earth performs water-sports in a pleasure-pool,
or in a river, or in a lotus-pond, in water that is pure and reaches up to his neck.
Square or perfectly circular, beautiful and adorned with steps,
whitened with lime, smooth, this enchanting pleasure-pool was captivating.
Or it may be surrounded by walls, or likewise by white-plastered houses,
or even by variegated curtains, or by most enchanting trees.
Adorned and exquisitely decorated with a variegated canopy,
it produces delight in the mind and removes the fever of the body.
One should fill [the vessels] with water from the flow of a water-wheel, or with water brought by female slaves,
using jars or leather bags purified with cloth.
One should cast fish without thorns into that pond,
and one should station swans and cranes there in the water.
He summoned young, beloved women who were skilled in reading the mind and captivating;
they were dressed in white garments and anointed with saffron.
Richly adorned with golden ornaments, decorated with flower-staffs,
these beloved women were clever, slender, and endowed with expressive gestures and amorous charms.
Others, whose minds were full of serene faith— his father, son, and domestic priest—
were clad in white garments and endowed with the conduct and principles of the wise.
And after more than one and a half yāmas had passed,
having approached the pleasure-pool and adorned himself with bright ornaments, he was decorated with golden jewels.
One should scatter flowers and pieces of camphor there;
the wise king, being skillful, should enter first for the sake of sport.
Having dragged some amorous women, embraced others,
placed some upon their shoulders, and pulled the garments of others;
Some he led inside by taking them by the hand, some by affectionate glances,
and others by means of respectful gestures, having ushered in his own wives.
Then, O protector of the earth, the Tathāgatas should be led by those skilled in water-sports into a very cool pleasure-pool.
Then, all those staying in the water, remaining within the liquid, seized the many pieces of camphor situated therein, each vying for precedence, saying, "I first, I first!"
The lord of the earth should scatter pure gold coins and various kinds of gems before them for the purpose of their acceptance.
Then, being repeatedly enticed, they plunge into the water again and again;
accompanied by their beloveds, one should observe their eager longing.
They all released long, heavy breaths, overcome with exhaustion;
their hair was disheveled, and their eyes were bloodshot.
Having placed the obtained jeweled necklaces in their mouths in that manner,
and seeing them again with their eyes opened wide, he was filled with laughter.
Beholding the face of his beloved, his mind overflowing with joy and having attained supreme bliss, he should dismiss everyone from the water.
Then those young women, their hearts overflowing with love,
shone together with the king like rivers with the ocean.
Just as female elephants are [protected] by the world-elephants, or as the hosts of apsarases are by Śakra;
or as the cowherd women are by Vāsudeva, or as the stars are by the moon.
Standing in the midst of the water like moving lotus-pools,
those lovely women shine with their lotus-faces in the auspicious water that reaches up to their necks.
These women sprinkle the lord of the earth with waters that mock pearls,
and they strike their beloved with flowers as if with the arrows of Love.
Some women, out of fear of the depth [of his passion], embrace the king around the neck and obtain extreme pleasure born from that close embrace.
Terrified by the touch of the fish, certain beautiful-faced women embraced the protector of the earth and attained the bliss residing within their hearts.
Under the pretext of wiping away the collyrium from the corners of her wide eyes,
she covers her own eyes while gazing at another with playful gestures.
By the pressing of feet, by the squeezing of each breast,
and by the drawing of the waist-knot against her body, the king may cause desire to awaken in her.
Thinking her face-lotus to be a lotus, I struck it;
O slender-limbed one, you are my beloved, so you ought not to be angry.
"O fair-hipped one, thinking it was a ruddy sheldrake, I have embraced your breast, which is reddened with saffron; O beloved, do not be angry with me."
From here, the protector of the earth, delighting all his most beloved ones with touches, glances, and conversation, should engage in water-sports.
The beloved women had breasts like ruddy geese, eyes that moved like fish,
faces like blooming lotuses, and arms like creeping vines of lotus stalks.
With deep navels that hold swirling eddies, these women are pools of the essence of beauty;
by their union, they cause the ocean of the king’s mind to swell.
A king immersed in the flavor of passion (anurāga-rasa), even while dwelling in the midst of water,
may cause his beloved women, who are permeated by the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), to sink.
Having struck [the water] with his hand, he stirred the water with his arm;
plunging repeatedly into the water, he sprinkled that water with his cupped hands.
Carrying the women across the water with his two arms,
the king sported as if lying upon a couch, resting playfully upon the surface of the water.
Thus, O lord of men, one should engage in water-sports for the sake of play in various ways—
whether in a pleasure-pool, a river, or a lotus pond.
Having concluded his water-sports when the day was somewhat remaining,
the king, having emerged from the water, should put on two excellent garments.
A wise person should adorn his body by anointing it with a paste mixed with saffron juice and embellishing it with applications of sandalwood.
Having fashioned a necklace of large pearls as an ornament for her neck,
she made an exquisite crest-ornament with jasmine and campaka blossoms.
Standing in the courtyard and sitting upon his bed,
he was surrounded by beloved women adorned with beautiful ornaments.
One should bestow various kinds of wealth upon those who accompanied her in the water-sports,
and likewise give many gifts, such as Chinese silk garments, to her beloved women.
Thus has the water-play, joined with the erotic sentiment, been described.
[Thus ends the water-play, verse 5.
Now, the grassy-plain play is being told by King Soma.
In that mass of clouds, which shone like Mount Añjana, resembled a herd of elephants,
and appeared like the thick column of smoke from the fire of desire;
Resounding with the roar of Kāmadeva’s chariot, like the trumpeting of rutting elephants,
delightful with the thunder of rain clouds and accompanied by the cries of peacocks;
[She was] like the brilliant, flickering lightning in the form of the sword of Manmatha,
raining down [showers] resembling flowers drawn forth by the flower-arrowed god.
Clad as it were in a garment of vast, multicolored hues produced by Indra’s rainbow, the quarters of the sky shone resplendently like beautiful brides.
Scented with the fragrance of Kadamba and Ketakī flowers,
and joined by a cool breeze cooled by the touch of the Lord of the Western Quarter.
When the rainy season had arrived— delightful, dispelling the affliction of wind and heat, increasing the sweetness of mango groves, and providing a dwelling for flocks of swans.
The grassy meadow, draped with dark blue cloths as it were, and strewn with numerous rubies like indragopas, shines resplendently.
In such delightful regions, the lord of the earth should engage in games upon the verdant meadows, which are enchanting to the hearts of women.
One should surround the area of the pavilion on all sides with beautiful curtains made of cloth dyed with kausumbha, arranged so as to extend upwards.
And at various places, multi-colored lutes (or flutes) should be installed;
these, rich with the hues of red ochre and other pigments, are enchanting with their silk-woven frames.
Having risen at dawn and performed his morning rites,
he then prepared himself with ornaments and was surrounded by his beloved attendants.
Having summoned a herd of female elephants, resounding with the tinkling of golden bells,
with vermilion applied to their foreheads and adorned with flowers;
Horses that were captivating to the mind, noble, graced by graceful gaits,
equipped with golden saddles, and made resonant by the tinkling of small bells.
O King, accompanied by his beloved, he should mount the female elephant at his side;
and the lord of the ladies of the inner apartments should cause the women to mount the mares in due order.
Then the king should cause the throngs of elegant women,
as well as the female singers, dancers, and excellent courtesans, to dismount from their horses.
Then, one should proceed very slowly and gracefully toward a grassy meadow;
having warded off other people, one should enter behind a screen of cloth.
Having seated the submissive cow, which was under his control, the lord of the earth descended;
thereafter, he caused his beloved women of the inner apartments to descend.
Then the king, the lord of his beloveds, should dispatch the women of pleasure to the small huts and pavilions equipped with lutes and flutes.
Various intoxicating drinks that are pleasing to the heart, food and delicacies that are charming to the mind,
fragrant flowers, betel leaf, and unguents.
One should send garments, fine jewels, and various ornaments to one's beloved wives, according to their degree of affection and honor.
Then he himself should eat, together with his sons and friends,
as well as servants whose hearts are full of goodwill, a meal that is both delicious and pleasing to the heart.
Having finished the meal, discarded the leftovers,
and sat down in a clean place, one should then perform the rite of adornment.
Having taken sandalwood mixed with moon-essence (kumkuma), smooth and light,
one should anoint the body until it is endowed with a brilliant luster.
Having put on yellow garments and being adorned with ornaments of pearls,
he applied a mark of sandalwood paste embellished with black musk.
Adorned with a crest-jewel as his head-ornament and wearing a crown of *ketakī* petals,
he should then summon his beloved women, who are themselves radiant with jeweled finery.
Their garments were dyed with great quantities of silver, vermilion, and lac;
their bodies were smeared with saffron, and they were adorned with colored staffs and water-pots.
With white necklaces of five strings, radiant with large pearls,
and with series of neck-ornaments as well as pearl crest-ornaments;
With bracelets made of pearls, with pearl ornaments for the parting of the hair,
with leaf-shaped pearl earrings, and with circular clusters of pearl buds.
Adorned and radiant, red-hued and fond of crimson garments,
these deities presiding over passion have arrived in person, having assumed embodied forms.
All of them should stand joyfully and playfully surrounding the king;
meanwhile, the king should have a troupe of female singers from among the Mātaṅgas sing from a distance.
Trivalī should play musical instruments that are enchanting with their various modulations;
and those beloved women, skilled in dance, should perform dances that are like creepers of affection.
And let the multitude of Caṇḍālas give gold and many garments;
then, dismiss that group defiled by the Mātaṅga lineage.
Then he should give to his beloved women divine garments, gold,
various ornaments, and betel-leaf held in their mouths.
Then, when the sun’s rays had grown faint, the king rose up and had a golden elephant-goad brought,
its two prongs bound with gold.
It was equipped with golden bells, adorned with a girdle of gold,
covered with saffron-dyed cloth, and beautifully decorated with the waistbands of heroes.
In the place where the sun has set, one should smear the area with vermilion paste and sprinkle the facial circle with a mixture of turmeric and rice flour.
Having smeared his limbs, including his head,
with oil and having mounted upon a single seat, the king should cause those beloved women, brought under his control, to ascend it as well.
Lifting up his head with his trunk, [he struck] with the tips of his beautiful fore-branches;
driving the excellent elephant forward with his pair of raised thumbs,
he held it at a certain spot on the ground and struck those standing before him.
"Releasing those who were being beaten, the king would go to his own palace.
Thus was the game of grassy meadows described by King Soma.
[Thus ends the game on the grassy meadow.
||6||] Now, the game with sand is described, endowed with its defining characteristics; it is a delight for the hearts of the virtuous, occurring when the clouds are thick and the rain falls heavily.
Resembling the radiance of Hara’s laughter, adorned with white clouds,
and filled with a multitude of swans, elephants, cranes, and peacocks;
At the end of the rainy season, which is the cause for the production of pearls,
[the sky] was tawny with the pollen of *śāli* rice flowers and reddish-brown with the filaments of lotuses.
When the wind was mild, cool, fragrant, and blowing from the northeast,
his mind— though turbid with envy— became as clear as if through endearing flatteries.
When the waters, turbid from the rainy season, have become clear through autumn,
the rivers— slender and dark-brown— are frequented by pairs of ruddy geese.
Near that [lake], the king should engage in sports that gladden the heart, where the lotus-stalks are like his arms and the moving pāṭhīna fish are his eyes.
In that water, which was pleasant to the touch, which removed the affliction of thirst,
which resembled fine pearls in appearance, and which possessed a luster like golden dust.
In a charming location covered by a cool curtain, upon a heap of smooth sand that shone like various clusters of jewels.
Having constructed a beautiful cloth pavilion and bamboo mats made of fine fabric,
and having put on white garments, he [entered] together with the women of the inner apartments.
Richly adorned with golden ornaments, the lord of men arrived there and approached the vicinity of the water, which brings clarity to both sight and mind.
Having sat down at a short distance, situated in the midst of a group of young women,
[he saw] circles and squares provided with four gates.
One should construct separate pleasure groves for the king,
by repeatedly throwing handfuls of water and soft earth.
One should throw [the water] outside as long as it does not reach clarity;
once the water has become clear, one should then throw in the aquatic plants.
One should place blue lotuses, red lotuses, and fragrant hundred-petaled lotuses there for the sake of beauty,
as well as many other flowers for their fragrance.
One should construct a beautiful enclosure wall or a temple made of heaps of sand,
provided with fine stairs and surrounded by a moat filled with water.
The king should show the overflow of water to his beloved women,
and they, in turn, should show him the reservoirs they themselves have constructed.
They should display their sweetness, fragrance, and coolness to one another;
under the pretext of drinking, the king should touch her sprout-like lower lip.
Under the pretext of applying cooling ointments, he should touch her two breasts upon seeing them,
as well as balls of sand shaped like round play-balls.
Having placed them upon cocks, one should have them fight with one another;
one should know that when one is shattered, it has been defeated, and that constitutes the defeat of the combatant.
One should mount the back of the conquered [elephant], pull its ears while holding them,
and if it flees, one should pursue it across a ground of fine sand.
Or he might cast him into the midst of sand;
for that king would experience the pleasure arising from such playful jesting.
Then, having stepped forward slightly and sprinkling one another with water,
the king, after thus engaging in play, should then perform the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Adorned with various divine garments and many kinds of jewel ornaments,
and having mounted either a female elephant or a well-trained male elephant, he departed.
Neither a horse nor a carriage is superior to going on foot, nor is a swing fashioned of gold,
nor a chariot yoked with horses, nor a comfortable seat made of jewels.
Or else, accompanied by a multitude of young women, he wanders on foot with laughter,
charming speech, and playful glances and gestures.
"One should please the heart of one's beloved and then enter one's own dwelling"—
thus was the game of playing with sand described by King Soma.
[Thus ends the game of sand.
Now, the delightful game of moonlight, which increases joy, is described;
it should be played during the brilliant bright fortnight of either Āśvina or Kārttika.
In spring or in the heat of summer, when the moon has risen more than half-full,
the sky appears as if made white by the surging currents from the Ocean of Milk.
The grounds seemed as if smeared with the thick mud of prostrations,
while the walls of the quarters appeared as if constructed from great crystals and precious stones.
In the nights filled with the abundance of camphor dust,
as if the moon had taken refuge in the minds of proud women to break their resentment.
In that [night] which causes the night-lotuses to bloom, which rivals the splendor of the day-lotuses,
which dispels the pride of darkness, and which surpasses the excellence of the day;
In the moonlight, the king should engage in amorous play that increases passion,
in a spacious and beautiful courtyard free from stones, pits, and hollows.
For on a ground smeared with cow dung and strewn with heaps of flowers,
he wore a thick, smooth, white garment hanging down to his knees.
Having girt his loins firmly, he should adjust the belt to its proper measure;
over that, he should fasten a cloth band adorned with a cluster of small bells.
Adorned with beautiful ornaments of various colors to grace the expanse of her hips,
his entire body was anointed with sandalwood paste, and he was marked with a tilaka of musk.
His ears were adorned with leaf-shaped ornaments smeared with chalk,
and his topknot was completely filled with garlands of jasmine and Arabian jasmine.
Having raised the *khompaka* firmly, one should wrap it with a thick band,
along with a beautiful, smooth chain fashioned from refined gold.
A sacred thread hanging from his shoulder down to the region of his belly, like that of Brahmā,
and two smooth bracelets on his wrists made of radiant gold.
The lion among kings should wear [the sword] on his forearms with both wrist-bands;
others, however, being well-disposed and fearful of moving too hastily, should wear it otherwise.
Adorned with beautiful attire and other ornaments that were not ostentatious—
five, six, eight, ten, or even nine— they set out.
One should employ as attendants those who are suitable for play and comfort, treating them equally on both sides;
one should not employ children, nor the very old, nor the corpulent, nor those afflicted by disease.
Having gathered a group of his own age, who are skillful, discerning, and experts in swift movement,
he should engage in play with them in a place that is entirely delightful.
In the other group, having appointed a wise man as the chief friend,
the beloved woman or the king should employ those who can turn between the two sides.
Having himself become a judge, he should observe their play;
he should establish two winning positions made with fifty bow-lengths.
By the mere touch of that place, victory becomes certain. Those belonging to other groups should touch him as he runs forward with the desire to conquer.
If another should touch him, or if someone else should be touched by him,
he would avoid that mutual contact and, by running away, reach the place of victory.
He touches that [spot] where victory for one side may occur;
this was a game devised by Hari in the past while he was wearing the dress of a cowherd.
Because it is like the moonlight (śaśiprabhā), it is therefore called Hariśaśī;
the wise man should draw squares everywhere, just like a chessboard.
In a level ground, one should construct squares measuring four cubits in both width and length;
one may make seven or five such squares.
And on the horizontal lines, one [mark] should be placed at each [intersection] by one who is unwearied;
there, one called the "brush" runs along the straight lines.
One should release the lines in that manner and touch those situated within the squares; all the horizontal lines and the brush (or the one holding it) should be handled with great care.

When one [number] enters all the squares, having bypassed those lines situated on the opposing side that are to be avoided, and having emerged from every square, it then enters once more; [that number is a magic square].
But when the neutral line is bypassed by the player,
if the opponent subsequently crosses over the squares in that same order, [the move is considered illegal].
Then victory belongs to those situated outside, while those touched [by the enemy] suffer defeat;
the defeated outsiders shall remain within the interior of the enclosure.

Those situated outside and inside would go forth; their victory or defeat is as previously stated. If those situated outside should continuously prevail for three times [the cycle], [then victory belongs to them].
Then those situated within would joyfully mount its back;
this is called Koṣṭhakrīḍā, which was performed by Govinda in ancient times.
And for the sake of sport with the beautiful cowherd girls,
he created various wonders by constructing an artificial fortress with walls as high as a man's chest.
Some would be positioned inside and some would stand outside;
the sages would be there with balls made of flowers and with staffs born of the mind of the gods.
Thus, filled with excitement, they strike one another;
they beat the king with flowers that have been fashioned into the shape of balls.
Because they play with beautiful garlands and staves fashioned from *kesara* flowers under the moonlight,
it is therefore called "Moonlight Play" (*jyotsnākrīḍā*).
The enchanting "Moonlight Play" (Jyotsnākrīḍā) has been described by Bhūlokamalla.
[Thus ends the Jyotsnākrīḍā.
Now, the excellent "Crop-Field Play" (Sasyakṣetrabhavā Krīḍā) is being told.
In that place, which was a mass of mines for blooming flowers, graced by lordly elephants in rut,
frequented by joyful cranes, and crowded with proud deer;
The splendor of the lotus-pools has vanished, the peacock feathers have fallen away,
and the place is crowded with men trembling under the assault of the ivory lutes.
In that place where the fire was served by people whose every limb was bristling with horripilation,
and which was rendered fragrant with the scent of jasmine, blue lotuses, and camphor;
Even though the breeze was cool, fragrant, and pleasant, it caused distress to the people;
yet, for the husband and wife, it brought about a firm embrace even without the presence of love.
When such a winter had arrived— one that provides for a long night those who are devoted to sensual enjoyment, and which is rich with ripening crops—
The king should engage in sport situated in a delightful field;
he should move about among the hidden grains which produce the illusion of parrots.
They aroused the curiosity of the women's minds,
being surrounded by a beauty of filaments shaped like *punnāga* and *kesara* flowers.

Are these bamboo stalks, coconut shells, lotuses, pearl-oyster shells, conch shells, and snakes merely the products of people’s delusion regarding golden grains—delusions worthy of their fathers? Or are they indeed [golden]?
They were adorned with pearls grown upon the ears of grain,
which, by their splendor, rivaled the beauty of the *saptacchada* tree.
It was adorned with yava grass stalks that shone intensely with their waves, appearing as if they were the very cause for the playful movements of the goddess Lakṣmī.
In a field rich with the beauty of greenery, delightful and pleasing to the sight,
where even in the absence of rain there arose a lush sward of young grass variegated by indragopaka insects.
It was adorned with wheat stalks resembling braided hair,
rich in blossoms and always covered by excellent leaves.
Resembling a row of lamps, with safflower at the tips of the flowers,
it was surrounded here and there by rows of cucumber plants laden with fruit.
Having diligently observed such delightful fields, variegated with ripe peas that were free from any blemish;
The king should provide for their protection through trusted attendants;
[he should offer them] curd-rice mixed with black pepper, cardamom, and fresh ginger.
A threshing floor of wheat, a heap of turmeric and sour gruel,
as well as cakes, sweetmeats, pancakes, and fried pastries.
The king should first dispatch milk-rice mixed with sugar, honey, buttermilk, and curds,
as well as fruits, roots, and tubers seasoned with mustard and salt,
along with various grains to the circle of the fields.
Furthermore, he should dispatch fattened pigs and rams;
then, accompanied by his beloved and attended by young women, he himself should proceed.
He should travel in comfortable vehicles accompanied by friends who are full of devotion, skilled in song, and likewise by Brahmins,
as well as by attendants dressed as guards for his protection.
Having reached a designated portion of the grain field, the lord of the earth,
having excluded other people, should enter together with those previously mentioned.
Having cleared away some crops there to provide space,
one should make that area spacious, quadrangular, and beautiful.
And one should place there a beautifully adorned lute prepared with fine cloth,
as well as some women of lovely appearance who are thick-set and have assumed a humble posture.
He saw heaps of dehusked barley, chickpeas, and various kinds of beans, as well as beautiful wheat ears, each wrapped in cloth.
Having brought many fruits of the karkaṭī with numerous servants,
the king should present them individually to the brahmins and their beloved wives.
Having given various kinds of cooked food and edibles, he should dismiss everyone;
then he should eat at his pleasure together with his sons and kinsmen.

Various kinds of meats roasted by fire,

Chickpeas roasted with hot sand, as well as other varieties,

That powder, combined with oil, along with ginger and cumin,

Resembling the outpouring of a garuḍa, resembling vaidūrya gems,

One should bring lovely women with slender limbs who captivate the heart through their affection;

On sandy banks overgrown with grass, within the sound of lutes and flutes for one's beloved,

Behind concealed curtains, made beautiful by various colors,
the chosen women should be stationed in rows according to their respective ranks.

as well as plates, goblets, and shells made of glass, gold, and silver.

Women should fill [the vessels] with liquors contained in hollowed hands;

In some [vessels] he should place blue lotuses, and in others jasmine flowers;

then, having prostrated to one another and received permission with joy, they should partake of the wine.
Eager for drink, the slender women would drink from their cups that which was white,

Having drunk ghee, they should drink that wine produced from sweet grapes and other fruits, which is predominantly slightly pungent and exceedingly intoxicating.

Women would eat various foods and consume chickpeas and the like;

They then described that wine, which was intense with pungent, sour, and other flavors,

One should not [employ] a dancer, nor likewise a singer, a chatterer, or a weeper; nor one who causes laughter, one who provides secret counsel, or incense that increases passion.
Drinking with great joy and recounting the virtues of their beloveds,
those excellent women, slightly intoxicated, resembled a cluster of blooming lotuses.
Some women with eyes resembling blue and red lotuses repeatedly mistook the reflection of a lotus for the actual flower and tried to brush it away.
Thus, mistaking it for a blue lotus petal,

They drink their own sweet [nectar], not noticing it,

A certain beautiful woman, fearing it might be a bee,
trembles as she quickly withdraws her hand from the shadow of her own nails, suspecting them to be petals of a ketaki flower.

Oh, how strange it was that for a certain woman, the ocean of passion arose from her husband;

It destroys the peace of mind, increases attachment like a friend toward those who possess gain,

Then their drinking was like that of those in distress;

Conversation devoid of respect is futile quarreling;

One woman dances joyfully with faltering steps;
another goes along, shaking her limbs, as she follows an unmarked path upon the ground.

Even while being agitated, the king experiences delight;
she is shameless, her two breasts exposed, and her garments removed.
Seeing the queen standing nearby, they departed with disciplined composure;

He shines, caressed by women through their pleasant touch,

Increasing their passion by drinking the essence of wine—

The two opposing, firm arrays (vyūha) should be stationed facing one another.
The wise man should place two chariots situated in the second house from the first sign.
In the space between those two, one should place a pair of horses;
beyond that, a pair of men, and in their midst, the king and his minister.
The two [elephants] with one foot raised should be especially stationed by the minister;
in the eight squares in front of them, he should place eight infantrymen.
In this manner, the supreme [practitioner] should perform the placement of his own powers in two rows;
the chariot moves along the diagonal, leaving an interval of one square.
The horse should move along the squares at the edges of the four corners;
the lord of elephants should proceed through the four paths and leap everywhere.
Whether moving one step, two steps, or even all [four], the practitioner, impelled by the wind,
indeed proceeds to all four nearby corners.
The king moves through all the directions in the adjacent squares;
he moves with one foot and strikes with two corners.
He always proceeds forward and never turns back; having gone through the fourfold sequence of steps and so forth, he shall become a mantra-master.
Just as a minister retreats after four steps,
so do the king, the minister, the chariot, the elephant, and the horse, each remaining within its own station.
A foot soldier (patti) moving from one square to another with his feet destroys the superior force stationed there;
however, a foot soldier standing at a double angle (dvikoṇa) destroys those who have gone before him.
Since the infantry protects the chariot from the direction of the [other] two divisions,
those who know the subject declare that one foot belongs to the chariot stationed at the corner.
When there is a reversal of one who has reached the seventh line, having [already traversed] four steps in the third and fifth lines;
