for one situated at the end of the row, there would be two *paras* of a chariot.
Thus has the placement of the chariot's feet been described;
for this horse standing at the corner-side, there are three feet.
In the second enclosure, there is a pair of feet at each corner,
four feet at the end of each side, and three feet for each horse at the corners.
In the second circle, another set of six words is recited;
and in the center, of the horse situated among these sixteen.
The eight steps have been specified by those skilled in the four branches [of medicine],
whether [the patient] is situated in his own place or located elsewhere.
Here, fourteen squares are described for one born under the Sāma Veda:
one square situated at the outer corner, and two squares located at the edge.
Furthermore, for one standing elsewhere than at the edge of the mantra [circle], there are four steps;
however, for a king standing outside the row, there are five steps.

In its corner, a three-square [space] is to be known; elsewhere, an eight-square [space] is mentioned. It is constructed by those who know the four divisions; then, of that [array], there are three squares for the foot-soldier.
The number of words has been declared by me as determined for the four sections;
the first array is called Sīma, and after that is Sumeru.
The third is called "cow-urine" (gomūtra); these arrays may be arranged according to one's preference.
In the "single-file" array, all the foot soldiers stand like a surging wave.
When the military array has been deployed, that is designated as the "boundary" (sīmākhya);
it occurs when the fourfold army is arranged in the shape of the peak of Mount Sumeru.
The array proclaimed as Sumeru is formed by the players;
it is so called because in that game the foot soldiers move about like the flow of cow's urine.
The "cow-urine" array has been taught by those skilled in horsemanship;
it consists of chariots, elephants, cavalry, and infantry, with the ministers positioned even closer than the king.
A wise king should diligently employ spies against the enemy army,
and he should likewise protect his own [kingdom], his ministers, and his elephants.
When this has been done, one should bind the supreme king in the place of the target;
the soldier in the fifth row, and the ministers in the sixth row.
On the seventh day, one should perform the chariot rite, which is known by the wise as the "vajra-bind" (diamond-bond),
wherein the mantra-practitioner and the warrior shall be mutual protectors of one another.
On the sixth day, the minister and the soldier [are present], while on the fifth there is firm binding;
where the excellent warriors are intent on protecting one another and seeking each other's welfare.
Like bodyguards in battle, they call that formation the "Bond" (Bandha);
it should repel the enemy army within its own fourfold array.
Having broken through the enemy's forces, the wise king should then enter the enemy's territory;
having bypassed the royal highway, he should place his own king there.
To conceal him, however, one should place a minister in front;
his protection from harm should be ensured by means of a chariot drawn by horses.
One who possesses mastery over the fourfold army will thus quickly achieve victory;
like a wise man, he should examine and then move that which is to be moved, such as a chariot and so forth.
One should deposit it only after examining it, in a place where no harm exists;
when it goes toward destruction, one should provide protection for it.
Therefore, having observed what exceeds [the prescribed measure], one should perform protective rites;
however, a king standing at the place of execution must never be killed.
The wise man should say, "Let the king go; he shall suffer death at your hands. One should say, "The king is to be killed," but not, "Let him kill another."
Having established [the king] in such a position, the wise ruler should,
with great effort, simultaneously provide protection for both the king and the elephant.
Since the king flees, the elephant must certainly be brought down;
he may be concealed by someone in the path of the elephants in whatever form is appropriate.
Likewise, one should not employ a double-edged weapon that strikes others;
for it is like an elephant-killer's covering, which, having struck the king in battle, [kills] him by its own recoil.
Then the king should strike down the enemy, for he becomes the one who destroys the elephant's standing ground;
thus the wise man should diligently create an obstruction to the path of the lord of men.
Having appointed the king’s executioners all around his own feet,
he should point out that the king is to be slain by someone else entirely.
Because that side is deprived of both movement and stability, it shall suffer defeat;
for what use are well-protected other warriors, or even a horse, a chariot, or an elephant?
Or the wise king should station a minister to block the path [of the enemy];
even then, the death of the king must be announced by someone else.
But if it rises while others are engaged in slaughter, there will be the defeat of the king's faction;
or else, his own army will stand firm, acting as a barrier on the king's path.
Nevertheless, when a king is pierced by anyone else, defeat occurs;
indeed, defeat is said to arise through these three modes alone.
[Thus ends the diversion of Caturaṅga.
Now another method of play called Sarvatobhadra is described.
When the king places his forces in one place while he himself remains alone elsewhere,
he moves like an elephant, like a chariot, or like a horse.
Like a minister or like a soldier, he is likewise appointed by the Khelaka to all his own positions throughout every station.
A king marches against, slays, and binds the enemy's forces;
therefore, a wise man should construct defenses to block his path.
Having gradually led his own army ahead for protection— with elephants, pairs of horses, chariots, ministers, and soldiers— he proceeded slowly.
One should cast him into a perilous position so that he becomes helpless;
when this is done, victory belongs to the leader who possesses strength in the game.
Otherwise, victory belongs solely to that lord of the earth;
in this application, the "fourfold movement" (caturaṅgakrama) is another secret.
It is stated by King Someśvara that the king should be moved by a group of six,
while the minister by a group of five.
An elephant moves with four steps; a horse gallops with three;
a chariot proceeds with two; and a foot soldier advances with one.
The wise, having performed the protective rites as before, should engage in play;
thus the game of *kelirekhā* proceeds with balls and two ball-players.
In each turn, there shall be a fall for both sides by rotation;
where there are four players (or throwers), there the array is determined.
The white and red forces should be arranged with a single interval between them;
the chariots are to be stationed at the corners, and then the horses to the south.
On the right side of the horses were elephants fashioned from ivory;
near them stood four kings, devoid of ministers.
"There is no rule here that a king must not be slain;
the downfall of the four [castes] has been declared, and it must be carried out again and again."
Having eaten what was desired and delicious, he was contented and joyful in mind;
[he ate] for the sake of vigor, for the sake of the stomach, and to dispel sleep and lethargy.
One should engage in the play of riddles, which increases wisdom,
having invited clever and wise men who are experts in the literary arts.
A king should employ wise men who are skilled in understanding riddles, eloquent, and deeply learned in determining the solutions to enigmatic questions.
One person asks and another answers; therein lies defeat for the ignorant. Riddles are manifold and produce wonder in men.
Certain questions regarding one's own nature, as well as others, cause even the minds of the learned to be agitated with curiosity.
The answers may be given individually or collectively, consisting of multiple-word phrases with various meanings;
they may contain inserted syllables that are meaningful, or inserted words that are meaningful.
Some have their answers already stated, while others follow the words as they were spoken;
some have syllables dropped, some have morae (mātrās) dropped, and likewise some have the bindus (anusvāras) dropped.
Some have reversed syllables, and some are known to have hidden meanings.
[Thus ends the inquiry into their essential nature:
Even when sent as a messenger, one does not fear; moreover, one shines with splendor.
Let it be explained what the "whorl of teeth" (radāvarta) signifies; it is said to be the source of fear.
How does a single wheel, whether with two feet or without horses, continue to roll?
It does not move even a single step; what is that entity called? Though it is one, it becomes manifold and manifests itself here and there.
Furthermore, that wise man understands how it returns to oneness;
though possessing wings, he does not fly away, nor does he run without feet.
Who is this being that sleeps while looking about? Let it be told;
he always moves with speed, and once gone, he does not return.
She both diminishes and increases; let that woman be identified!
For half a day her body diminishes, and for half a day it increases.
Let a name be assigned to her whose complexion is dark;
she for whom two [teeth] are white, two are small, and two have fallen upon the earth.
"Let this creature be examined: it always moves with two long legs;
it is capable of bearing a great burden and always travels on eight feet."
Let the name of that which moves with effort by means of two [organs] be determined;
those who desire the welfare of both worlds call the living being (jīva) by a single name.
"O wise one, let those two who are untouchable be identified by name;
they cannot be seen with the eye, nor is their sound heard when they speak."
Even though deprived of life, it still moves; tell me, if you have the skill, what is its root, its branches, its fruit, and its leaves?
It has its roots above and its branches below; its root is its fruit and its leaf.
"It cannot be taken away by anyone; tell me, where does it stay?
It touches the limbs while remaining invisible, and once it has clung to them, it cannot be removed."
Having entered the place where the mat was, he whose life-force was sustained—indeed, who is there that does not exist?
Though handless, he splits the stone; and without feet, he runs.
A woman roars without a mouth; who is she? Let her be identified by name.
With its crest (or tuft), that utterly pure one drinks those [waters] with its tail (or hindquarters).
What object is it that quickly makes even a back appear graceful? Let it be revealed:
through its possession, even a steadfast man becomes unfit for service and constantly roars.
O King, who indeed would fight even when accompanied by armies,
having covered his mouth, bound his limbs, and expanded his inner consciousness?
"He speaks clearly; he is a base man. O learned one, tell me: how is it that one of these two remains within their wombs in the form of an embryo?"
A fool, when expelled with effort, kills his parents at that very moment;
a son, though produced with great care, may himself become the slayer of his father.
He who knows that he himself is being slain by his own father is wise;
likewise, a wife who is pleasing to look upon and graces the hands and feet is truly beneficial.
"O wise ones, tell me: who is it that immediately pursues his desires?
A dull-witted person runs swiftly after them, while one of good conduct flees from the crooked lord."
He who knows that even the stainless is possessed of impurity is a wise man. By what are beings devoid of effort born? By what do they live?
By what means does a beautiful woman steal the heart? Let the wise declare this.
Which woman on this earth is to be praised, and which is to be censured?
Let those who know it examine and determine that which is known by its qualities and has resorted to a single name—
that by which the stability of the elders is maintained and by which their suffering is warded off.
Tell me, who has come to your home, that by which the life of kings is sustained; in what [circumstance] is the fruit of giving obtained, and in what [place] should one take food?
In which [place] would one who is delighted fall? Tell me that, O wise one!
These meanings of the half-verses with inserted syllables...

Upon which messenger would the gaze fall? Tell me this, O wise ones!

O wise one, when the arrow is drawn to the ear and the target is struck, make the food well-prepared and firm;
join it with the letter placed in the middle.
For the sake of life, for the sake of modesty, and for the sake of aesthetic flavor, compose your work with care;
for a composition that is neither too concise nor too prolix is neither disjointed nor ruined.
A king who conducts himself with heroic virtue should strive to avoid these two [types of people]:
one who is like a crow at the edge of a threshing floor, and one who speaks excessively even though he knows this [dharma].
What should be done when weapons fall and among children?
O wise one, by omitting the first and last letters, make the word "kṣam" meaningful.
Having placed the syllables at the beginning of the hair-pores and the phoneme at the end,
recite them twice and make the three words meaningful.
...the answer has already been stated.
What kind of being shines forth? [The answer is: *bhūtapah* (the lord of beings). What is said regarding a Brahmin at a *śrāddha* ceremony? [The answer is: *vipra* (a learned one).

May the three— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— the granter of desires, born of desire, and the destroyer of desire, who are omnipresent through time— protect King Soma.
What, when held up, quickly becomes a king? Who is served by people?
"Missing syllables"—

Two firm arrays should be positioned facing one another.
The wise man should place two chariots situated at the corners of the first square.
In the interval between those two, one should place a pair of horses;
beyond that, a pair of foot-soldiers, and in their midst, the king and his minister.
The two foot-soldiers should especially be stationed one-step apart by the practitioner;
in the eight squares in front of them, he should place eight foot-soldiers.
Thus, the supreme [practitioner] should perform the placement of his own powers in two rows;
the chariot moves along the diagonal, leaving a single square-interval between them.
The horse should move along the squares at the edges of the four corners;
the lord of elephants (the elephant) should proceed through the four paths and leap everywhere.
Whether taking one step, two steps, or even all of them, the practitioner, being impelled by the wind,
indeed moves toward all four adjacent corners.
The king moves through all the directions in the adjacent squares;
with one step he moves, and with two corners he strikes.
He always moves forward and is never turned back; having traversed the fourfold sequence of steps and so forth, he becomes a mantra-master.
Just as a minister retreats when the four positions are lost,
so too do the king, the minister, the chariot, the elephant, and the horse remain fixed in their respective places.
An infantryman moves from one square to another on foot and strikes the superior force stationed there;
however, when standing at a double angle (dvikoṇa), he slays those who have gone ahead of him.
Since the *sainaka* arises from the two feet (*dvipādāḥ*),
it is said by those who know it to be one foot of a chariot situated at the corner, for it is skillful in its protection.
When there is a reversal of one who has reached the seventh line, having [passed through] four steps in the third and fifth lines;
For one who has traveled by another path, the seventh [digit] becomes two feet;
for one situated at the end of the row, the chariot consists of two [other] digits.
Thus has the placement of the chariot's feet been described;
as for the horse standing at its corner-side, it has three feet.
The pair of feet of the one situated in the corner [is placed] at the end of the four feet;
in the second enclosure, in the corner, there are three feet of the horse (the four-footed being).
In the second circle, another group of six words is recited;
and [this applies] to the horse situated in the midst of these sixteen.
The eight steps have been specified by those expert in the four branches [of yoga],
whether one is situated in one's own place or located anywhere else.
Here, fourteen squares are described for the birth of the *sāman*:
one square for that situated in the outer corner, and two squares for that situated at the edge.
Furthermore, there are four steps for one standing elsewhere from the edge of the mantra;
however, for a king standing outside the row, there are five steps.

In its corner, a three-square space is to be known; elsewhere, an eight-square space is mentioned. That [space] was constructed by those who know the four divisions; then, of that [array], there are three squares.
I have declared the number of words determined for the four sections:
the first array is called Sīmā, and after that is Sumeru.
The third is called "Cow's Urine" (gomūtra); these arrays may be arranged according to one's preference.
In all of them, the foot soldiers stand in a single row like a surging wave.
When the military array is deployed in such a manner, it is designated as the "boundary" (sīmā).
When the fourfold army takes the shape of the peak of Mount Sumeru, [it is called the "peak" array].
In this game, the array known as Sumeru is formed by the players;
in this play, the foot soldiers move about like the flow of cow's urine.
The "Array of Cow-Urine" has been taught by those skilled in the four divisions of the army;
it consists of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry, with ministers positioned even closer to the king than the foot soldiers.
A wise king should diligently employ a double stratagem against the enemy army,
while protecting his own [kingdom], his minister, and likewise his elephant.
When this has been done, one should fix the supreme king in the position of the target (the center);
the soldier in the fifth row, and the ministers in the sixth row.

On the seventh day, one should form the chariot array; this is known by the wise as the "thunderbolt-binding" (vajrabandha), wherein the minister and the warrior serve as mutual protectors for one another.
On the sixth day, the minister and the soldier are present; on the fifth, there is firm bondage.
Wherein the excellent warriors, desiring mutual welfare, provide protection.
Like bodyguards in battle, they call that formation the "Bond" (bandha);
by means of it, one should ward off the enemy army within one's own fourfold array.
Having broken through the enemy's forces, the wise king should then enter the enemy's territory;
having bypassed the royal highway, he should station the king there.
To conceal him, however, one should place a minister in front;
one should have his afflictions avoided by means of a chariot drawn by horses.
One who possesses mastery over the fourfold army will thus quickly achieve victory;
the wise man, having deliberated, should set in motion that which is to be moved, such as a chariot and so forth.
One should deposit it only after examining it to ensure that no harm will arise;
if it should lead to injury, one must take measures to protect against it.
Therefore, having observed what is excessive, one should exercise restraints;
a king standing at the place of execution must never be killed.
The wise man should say, "Let the king go; he shall suffer death at your hands. One should say, "The king is to be killed," but one must not kill him oneself as another might.
Having established [the king] in such a position, the wise plaything-maker must diligently provide protection for both the king and the elephant simultaneously.
Since the king flees, the elephant must certainly be brought down;
he may be concealed by someone in some manner within the elephant-path.
Likewise, you should know that an intellect which causes harm to others must not be employed;
for this [intellect] is like an elephant that strikes its own coverer, if it were to abandon the king in battle.
If the king should strike another [elephant] at that time, it would become a cause for the elephant's death;
therefore, the skilled [trainer] should diligently prevent the king from obstructing its path.
Having appointed the king's executioners at his feet on all sides, one should declare:

Because that side is deprived of both movement and stability, it is defeated;
for what indeed can well-protected enemy warriors, a horse, a chariot, or an elephant do?
Or the wise king should station a minister to block the king's escape;
even then, the king's death must be announced by someone else.
If, however, they rise up for the sake of killing one another, there will be the defeat of the king's faction;
or else, his own army may stand firm, acting as a barrier on the king's path.
Nevertheless, when the king is pierced by anyone else, defeat occurs;
indeed, defeat is said to arise only through these three modes.
Regarding the game called Caturaṅga, that which pertains to the fourfold division [is thus described].
[This concludes the diversion of Caturaṅga.

When the king has his forces deployed in one place while he himself is alone elsewhere,
he then moves like an elephant, like a chariot, or like a horse.

One should cast him into a perilous position so that he may become powerless;
when this is done, victory belongs to the leader who possesses strength in the game.

for in that application, there is another method involving the four divisions of the army, which must be kept secret.
It is stated by King Someśvara that a minister should be moved [to another office] after six royal grants,
provided he has received five grants.
An elephant moves with four [feet], a horse gallops on three;

The wise should perform the play as before, having first established protection;

In each turn, there shall be a fall for both sides in alternation;
where there are four players (or throwers), there the array is determined.
The white and red forces should be arranged at intervals of one;
the chariots are to be stationed in the corners, and then the horses to the south.
On the right side of the horses were elephants fashioned from ivory;
near them stood four kings, devoid of ministers.
"There is no rule here that a king must not be slain;
the downfall of the four [classes] has been declared, and it must be carried out again and again."
Whosoever it may be, the great warriors and others are to be slain by the scribes (or playboys);
yet, when only one among them remains in the midst of the army, he is spared.
Then, by the calculation of turns from the movement of the lines, victory shall occur.
An odd number is considered for infantry, while an even number is prescribed for chariots.
A horse is declared to be of threefold value, while an elephant is of fourfold value;
a protector of the earth is of sixfold value—such is the consideration of numbers regarding the wager.
One should predict victory for him whose strength is superior;
one should know defeat for the inferior; and when they are equal, it is declared to be equal.
This rule has been prescribed by those skilled in the writing (or playing) of the four pieces.

two should be placed on the head, and one immediately after that.

Starting from the second house, one should place two [deities] of a single caste in each house,

Even these twelve [syllables] shall become one, with a single essence at the head;
thus was the arrangement of the *poṭalikā* described by King Soma.
On the two-headed [structure], four sārikās should be installed separately;
those three, excluding the one at the top, should be installed on the five houses.
In the twelfth [verse], there should be five syllables of the previous meter; then again, another *paṅkti* interval.
In the tenth house, there are four; this is the arrangement for the *madhyāntarasārikā*.
The two *sāryas* should be placed on the head; in the sixth [position], there are five other syllables;
likewise, three in the eighth, and five of the preceding syllables in the twelfth.
The arrangement of other *sārīs* is exactly the same;
this is the prescribed method for placing the *sārīs* during the game of *golaka*.
Two auspicious dice should be fashioned from ivory; they should be square, symmetrical, smooth, and shaped like elephant tusks. They should be made with the tips of the index fingers.
On the four sides of those two, dots in the shape of sesame seeds should be made for the purpose of indicating their respective shares;
their locations are now described.
Then, at the corners of the square, that group of five is proclaimed;
at the ends of the perimeter, two drops resembling vajras are called the pair.
One who is skilled in the game of sāri should know that three [sāris] are to be given: those resembling a group of five in the middle, and those resembling a vajra at both ends.
One should place two [units] between two [others], forming a network of dots with the brilliance of lightning;
one who is expert in the rules of *dāya* should know that as the "quadruple" (*catuṣka*) *dāya*.
Two pairs of twos, two pairs of threes, likewise two pairs of fours,
and two sets of fives— these are proclaimed as the equal groupings.
The distribution is two and three, two and four, and likewise two and five;
then three and four, and another distribution is three and five.
The fourfold and the fivefold—these ten types of throws (dāya) have been proclaimed.
By means of these throws, those skilled in gambling should engage in the play of dice.
One should make a square and a sphere of globular form;
there, the wise man should place a dot on each of the six sides.
Indeed, those numbering one, two, three, four, five, and six are, in sequence:
one is called a *bindu*, while the others are known as *sandhyā*s.
A man should cast the dice upon the ground so that they move,
as well as the two balls and the two pāśakas, without partiality.
Gama, cara, vivara, vibandha, and likewise pratibandha—
because the sārasa birds move swiftly through these, it is therefore called gama.
That which moves from here and there is called "cara" (the moving);
the binding that serves to obstruct its movement is known by the wise as "nibandha" (binding).
The bondage that obstructs even that [liberation] is called "obstruction" (pratibandha).
Thus, the Sārīkhela [bandha] is proclaimed to be fourfold by name.
And regarding the stationary and the moving [positions], as well as their continuations and non-continuations,
the sequence of play will be explained by Bhūlokamalla Deva.
In that regard, the superior movement is said to be without a point of departure or extension;
and those [vital airs] situated in the head, which are to be projected, must be moved by one desiring the movement.
One should swiftly lead the piece lacking beauty (the *apaśrī*) with force to quickly defeat those situated there;
the *sārī* (the piece with beauty), repeatedly maneuvering it, should be led with effort and speed.
One should strike the strings of others while protecting one's own strings;
one should cause all the strings to enter within the fifth house.
One should not keep a female bird in a house on the sixth or even the fifth day;
one who desires victory in battle should not engage in minute scrutiny.
A double distribution must never be made, for by that delay is caused;
one should not act with procrastination, since it leads to the destruction of the journey.
One who knows the calculation of the *svarī* should deliberate upon the discourse of inheritance;
thus employing it with wisdom, one attains swift victory.
Whether a binding or a wandering is being performed by another,
a man should perform both the wandering and the binding during his journey.
One should employ the *cara* when the *gamakheḷa* is bound; victory comes when the *cara* is present in the bound *śīrṣa*.
Even if only the *śīrṣa* is bound, there is no victory, for the *cara* is the cause of victory.
Having diligently fixed [the numbers] on the fourth, fifth, and seventh houses,
the knower who applies effort will become victorious in the game of *carakhela*.
And because the player's own sāris are destroyed when he binds the third or fifth house,
[the game is lost].
One who is deprived of the "head-binding" (śirobandha) is then known as a "fragmentary mover" (khaṇḍacara);
such a fragmentary mover is inferior, and victory in gambling with him is uncertain.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the complete *sāricara* (bowing);
an expert in binding should tie the two *sāryas* upon the head.
But others, staying diligently in their own houses wherever they may be,
should construct five houses, two by two, without any interval between them.
The sages do not emerge from this; the connection consists of retention.
In that way, the bond should be established so that there is the flow of saliva.
But when the connection is too close, one proceeds with only a single inheritance;
therefore, those who desire victory should not form such a close connection.
Thus the obstruction has been described; now the counter-obstruction is being stated:
one should effect the counter-obstruction among those who are self-possessed and of middling capacity.
All the characteristics of the *nibandhana* (binding) should be applied here as well, according to reason:

Resembling the bud of a lotus, like unto an elephant, a monkey, or a boar,
possessing a mass of bees, and having a luster equal to the throat of Śiva.
Resembling the splendor of Balabhadra’s younger brother, possessing the luster of the waters of the Yamunā,
resembling the cloudless sky, and having a brilliance like that of the embers of a fire.
It was like the night devoid of the moon, dark as musk, shining with a luster like the back of a black antelope,
and resembling the god of love.
In such a dark and smoke-filled chamber,
she then removed everything that might cause her feet to stumble.
Having summoned his own beautiful women, who were like dark-complexioned goddesses,
the lord of the earth should then begin the play and restrain their bashfulness.
He should cause boys about nine or eight years of age— skillful, experts in play, clever in jesting, and unobserved— to enter within.
Moving slowly and stealthily with their footsteps concealed,
the young men threw off the garments of some and seized the ears of others.
For some there was the pulling of their tresses; for some, the striking of their heads;
for some, the seizing of their braided hair; and for others, the beating of their backs.
For some there was the scratching of limbs, for others the threatening of fingers;
for some the dragging of feet, and for others the pressing of breasts.
One should employ some of them by instilling confidence through distorted and indistinct syllables, making them clever yet devoid of courtesy, and thus directing them accordingly.
Commanded by the king, they stood near them and performed,
exactly as they had been instructed by the monarch, such wonders that they caused amazement.
Some women, being embraced, let out cries like those of female dogs;
others, struck by their lovers, strike back at those standing nearby.
Struck by one whose name she does not know, she reviles him;
hearing abusive words that insult everyone, someone becomes enraged.
O proud woman, let the insult be given to him by whom you were struck;
for you yourself stand at my side—who else could strike me?
"O slender-waisted one, if I strike you with my head when it is devoid of its whiteness,
then surely you have been struck by her with whom you share this jest."
Thus, with great passion, those two struck the deer-eyed women on their heads and on the ground; they seized them by the hair and threw them against their necks and sides.
Thus, when a great clamor arose, the king— who nourished laughter and erotic sentiment— forced his way out by sheer strength, even though he was being restrained with great effort.
Hearing his laughter, their beloveds became overwhelmed with anger; thereupon they uttered insults, as if manifesting the full power of the god of love.
Some, seized by their hair, and others whose breasts were touched, are running toward the place of the wrestling match; by whom have I been insulted?
Some of those fawn-eyed women, stumbling as they ran, did not even look ahead;
by that very act, O Kuntalā, you were drawn toward him as he fell upon you.
Hearing such conversation between the two, which resembled the syllables of a mantra for the Great Goddess,
the protector of the earth would stop them with a laugh.
Hearing the sound of laughter, the passionate woman, overcome with anger,
gives him a reproachful and lustful insult.
Out of eager curiosity, the king rose quickly from his bed;
out of pride, he strode with straight steps, touching each of the boys' necks one by one.
Dragging the mass of flowers from one woman’s braid,
and crushing the dense, uplifted orb of another’s breast.
Having placed her sprout-like hand upon the cheek of another, she [placed it] upon the hip-region of yet another,
which was adorned with a golden girdle.
The neck of one woman was adorned with a pearl necklace,
while the lovely lower lip of another had the appearance of a ripe bimba fruit.
Touching the navel region of one woman—
which was deep and situated between her low and middle [stature]— the king experienced a surge of joy in his heart.
One should increase the joy arising in the heart of oneself and even of those who possess clear vision;
likewise, one should press the beautiful girdle against the pair of breasts.
The king was thus held by the hand of the slender-limbed woman,
who, with intense longing, grasped his hand and drew it toward her like a sprouting leaf.
If one who is capable [should] release the arm of one who is incapable and bound— which is as delicate as a *śirīṣa* flower—
and thereafter strike another with his foot;
She too, seizing his foot and being greedy for the concealment [of her body], would embrace him around the neck; yet another woman, out of jealousy, would pull away his arm.
In the duel between those two created by Kandarpa,
having escaped from the noose of arms, one would take refuge with another [weapon].
Then, having pulled at her garment and intent on flight,
you were seized again and again by her very hair.
Thinking, "By that very voice, another woman has been supported by him upon the mass of her hair as if she were the Earth;
and by him, I too have been supported through love alone," I was thus deluded by passion.
Just as she becomes face-to-face with the king for an embrace,
he, seeing her intent on seizing his hair, becomes enraged at her.
When their combat had proceeded hand-to-hand with hair-pulling, he emerged from there;
he should likewise issue such a command to all the other women as well.
Then, having gathered together and being intent on searching for him,
they all went to every place where the king might make a sound.
Upon hearing that sound of anklets, the king moved to another spot; then, each of his beloved wives individually recognized the distinct tinkling of her own small bells.
Some lovely [pillars] were provided with four corners at the place of the bed,
while others, standing upon each pillar, looked out in every direction.
Then that lord of the earth was embraced by all of them,
[touching him] on the hands, the head, the neck, as well as the chest and the feet.
From the pleasant touch of every limb and member, the lord of the earth,
having simultaneously attained supreme joy, becomes shaken in his mind.
Having experienced the sovereign empire of a mass of bliss through the play of darkness, the king,
having attained supreme delight, shines exceedingly.
Thus has the play of *timira* been described by King Soma.
[End of the *timirakrīḍā*, verse 17. Now the heroic play (*vīrakrīḍā*), which is captivating to the wise, is being told.
Success in one's undertakings was previously made manifest by men through play;
therefore, this [practice] should be performed by heroic men and not by other kings.
That [deed] was performed by the great adventurer Śūdraka, who took the form of Vikramāditya and was the foremost among heroes.
It was revealed by Vīranātha, the king Śālivāhana,
and also served by Kālidāsa, the son of the Lord of Kāntī.
And by other various heroes who sported upon the surface of the earth,
all of them attained great accomplishment through this very play.
A sword, an arrow, a mace, a vessel, a staff, a fist, a shield, a cloth, a mat, collyrium, sandals, a red jewel, a vetāla, a finger-ring, and an elixir.

Whether unliberated or liberated, the mace held in whose hand constantly slays excellent elephants— this is known as the accomplishment of the mace (gadāsiddhi).
The vessel that remains in one's hand grants all desired things;
this is declared to be the perfection of the vessel (pātrasiddhi), which bestows the fruit of all desires.

Whatever is touched by the hand, or whatever is perceived by the sight, or whatever is conceived by the imagination and stands before one—that very thing quickly comes to be; that is the perfection known as Yaṣṭi.
Whatever object one takes with the fist shall become gold;
this is declared to be the Fist-Perfection (Muṣṭisiddhi), which destroys the poverty of the world.
By merely wearing this [cloth], a person becomes invisible;
this is declared to be the perfection of the cloth, which deceives the sight of people.
Whether it be a living being or a non-living thing, whatever is drawn upon the ground, that very thing quickly comes to be; this is the accomplishment of the *khaṭi*.

When one whose eyes are smeared with collyrium sees even that which is bound as if it were unbound, or sees even that which is situated in water [as if it were not], it is due to the perfection of the application of the collyrium through the power of non-delusion.

Death itself does not arise from poisons, planetary influences, fire, or weapons;

It turns iron into gold and makes even the body free from old age and death;
such is this elixir, for it is through it that the perfection of the elixir is attained.
One certainly sees and obtains whatever object is situated within the earth;

Whatever gift one thinks of or requests that the die bestows upon him—

When a man, having become pure, speaks after forming a resolution in his mind, that becomes certain; this is called the perfection of speech (vāk-siddhi).
Therefore, this ritual procedure for weapons and mantras should be performed by one who is a great hero, endowed with the prowess of a tiger among beings, steadfast, pure, and virtuous.
When half a watch of the night has passed and the city is devoid of movement,

Remembering the god Narahari, the destroyer of all planetary afflictions,

Having held Caṇḍikā, the destroyer of all enemies, within his heart,

The vast banyan tree and the very extensive pippala tree,

The Piśācas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and the great hosts such as Vetālas;

[He saw] those with flaming mouths, massive bodies, and eyes shaped like the form of the bodiless god (Aṅga);

Those with drooping lips, drooping ears, and drooping noses, as well as those with pendulous bellies—
laughing distortedly or together, shrieking loudly, or clearly weeping.
Seeing those deformed beings of such a kind, the hero, filled with joy,

Some there have become servants, gratified by meat;

Having seen such valor, daring, and formidable strength of the king,

The yoginīs also arrived, intent upon the propitiation of the corpse;
there were many kinds of yoginīs there, born from their own fields, not born from a womb, and produced from the field.
Those born together, those arisen from the pledge, and those that are secret as well as manifest—
thus [is] the seat Jālandhara, and the second is Kāmarūpaka.
Uḍḍiyāṇa is the third, and Ujjayinī is remembered as the fourth;
Kolhāpura is the principal field (kṣetra), and Kara-Hāḍa is extensive.
Virāṭapura, Pūrṇagiri, Śrīgiri, Vimukoṭaka, Ambhūśikhara, Kaṅkeviñja (Śambhuśikhara), Vindhya, Citrakūṭa, and Nihāsaka.
Ekāmraka, Mahāciñcā (or Mahācīna), Prayāga, and likewise Malaya, as well as Kailāsapura and Palli— such are the sacred fields (kṣetra).
The Yoginīs born there are known as *ayonija* (not born from a womb) and *pīṭhajā* (born from sacred seats).

The Yoginīs born in the field (*kṣetra*) are known as *kṣīrajā* (born of milk) or *kṣetrajā* (born of the field). Others are those who have performed practice through another birth, regardless of where that birth occurred.
The Yoginīs, endowed with various powers, are considered to be innate (sahajā);
likewise, the Yoginīs follow the conduct of the pledge (samaya) through the initiation of the pledge.
The Yoginīs arising from the *samaya* are proclaimed to be of two kinds:
those born of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), those born of the fields (*kṣetra*), and those who are innate (*sahaja*).
They are described as being of two kinds, according to the distinction between secret and public:
the wife, the slave-girl, the courtesan, the widow, and the female ascetic.
Unperceivable through their own karmas, those five classes are said to be hidden;

the Ḍākinīs, the Pūtanās, the Śākinīs, and likewise the Rūpikās.

[Thus ends the Vīrakrīḍā || 18 ||] The play of love (premakrīḍā) is now described by Bhūlokamalla Deva:
"Knowledge is obtained through practice; wisdom is not obtained through yoga."
Wealth is obtained through industry; dharma is obtained through compassion and the like;
liberation is attained through the destruction of merit and demerit; and victory is obtained through prowess.
Health is obtained from medicine; long life is obtained from elixirs;
success is obtained from laughter; and the accomplishment of one's purpose is obtained through skillful means.
Through policy, a kingdom is obtained, as well as the increase of revenue for one who lives and possesses subjects;
through valor, fame is attained; and through wealth, great splendor is acquired by men.
Servitude is obtained through forgiveness; friendship through pleasant speech;
wives are acquired through marriage; and likewise, sons are obtained from wives.
Light is obtained from a lamp, beauty is obtained through ornaments,
cooking is achieved by fire, and water is obtained by digging.
From water, nourishment is obtained; from the cloud, rain is received;
from food, satisfaction is attained; and likewise, jewels are obtained from mines.
Elephants are captured by means of snares; fish are caught with hooks;
deer are lured by the cries of hounds; and birds and monkeys are trapped by deceptive disguises.
Grain is obtained from crops, fruit is obtained from a garden;
worlds are attained through gifts, and everything is attained through austerity.
Thus, all this that is desired is obtained through the exertion of a wise person;
yet, without merits performed in the past, even with love and effort, it is not obtained.
The love characterized by self-conceit is said to be the first; the second is that which is based on practice;
another is that consisting of conviction; and the fourth is indeed that which pertains to sense objects.
The notion that "sons, friends, and servants are mine," or that "servants and friends are mine"—
the attachment arising from these three temporal states is what constitutes conceit (*ābhimānikī*).
Just as there is a long-term attachment to one's home, village, city,
and so forth, and likewise a threefold affection for a wife, that [affection] for women is the highest form of habitual conditioning.

Or, one who has practiced [the notion of beauty] conceives it as such; that which appears due to similarity based on certain parts, such as the production of affection toward women, would be of the nature of conviction (*saṃpratyayātmikā*).
By the mere sight of her form, desire expands within the mind;
and by hearing her voice, the god of love blossoms in the heart.
Possessing a divine fragrance of the body, which, when smelled, bestows perfection upon the mind;
it occupies a place in the mind, being a beautiful vessel of radiant form.
By the mere tasting of her lower lip, which was fragrant with the essence of nectar,
his heart was revived by desire and inflamed by the fire from Śiva’s eye.
From the touch of the limbs and minor members, the fish-bannered god (Kāma) rises up;
that pleasure which increases in one's mind is indeed sensual.
When joy arises toward an object of sense, what further flavor or service could there be? That joy which possesses the highest excellence is called love.
Those pleasures which arise from conceit and repeated practice, as well as those consisting of conviction—
these may exist where pleasures derived from sense objects are not found.
Through the conjunction of great merit, passion arises for excellent women who have been desired in former births by those whose karma was previously accumulated.
The ripening of karma is difficult to ward off, as is that which arises from the mind associated with it;
for even when one is not in union, the God of Love, though burnt away, still instills affection.
In this world, the power of each individual is distinct;
whatever is desired by someone arises from practice performed in previous lives, such that even one who is censured may become impassioned.
A divine sapphire is seen grasping a blade of grass,
while a ruby remains naturally situated upon the head of a serpent.
Pure, cool, and sweet water does not please the submarine fire;
salty, tasteless water is pleasing to the fire of the ocean.
The moonlight arising from the nectar-rayed moon, which brings delight to all,
does not please the lotus born from the mud.
The cātaka bird rejoices in the rain-cloud of the monsoon;
the swans never rejoice in that very same cloud.
Touched by the rays of the moon, the elephant (or Death) does not shatter;
yet, by their mere contact, the moonstone would flow with water.
When the thousand-rayed sun has risen, there is an expansion for the eyes of the world,
while the blue lotuses, the friends of the eyes, undergo contraction.
For even though he knows the defect while his mind is being tormented,
he nevertheless delights for a moment out of love arising from deeds performed in a previous birth.
A beloved who has long been familiar may not please someone at first;
yet, through some fortunate conjunction, she alone may become the one dearer than life.
Affection arises somewhere through merit performed in a previous life, or through the excellence of a particular moment, or even from a connection of debt.
Once it has arisen, love is acquired in two ways:
through envy, which is difficult to obtain, and through restraint, as in the case of a village.
Just as liberation comes through the satisfaction of a Brahmin’s lifespan, and as one devoted to merit acts according to his life-span,
so too does affection arise among kings through envy.
Having bowed incessantly to liberation, what wonder is described therein?
That suffering is found in envy and the like, while happiness is found in love—that is truly marvelous.
In spring, there is the spotless moon, the southern Malaya breeze,
ornaments of fine jewels, and variegated garments.
Fragrant garlands, divine perfumes and ointments,
betel-leaf enriched with camphor, and food that is both pleasing to the heart and appetizing.
There is the most excellent Nandana grove, enchanting pleasure-pools,
houses perfected by nectar, and beds that bring the bliss of celestial touch.
There were delightful foods, the ground was covered with glass mosaics,
the palaces were provided with canopies, and there was incense made from black aloe-wood.
Sweet sounds of song, the resonance of the lute and the flute, and dances imbued with emotional expression awaken him who is united [in yoga].
The poem abounds in the erotic sentiment; the narrative arises from amorous enjoyment;
the assembly brings pleasure to the ears; and it is endowed with the name "Hāsya" (the Comic).
A young woman endowed with beauty, possessing the noble grace of expansive playfulness,
full of passion and a moist (intense) heart, and overflowing with skill in the arts.
All these things that bring happiness are, in the ultimate sense,
created by the Supreme Lord solely as instruments for the cultivation of love.
The supreme essence and entire wealth of saṃsāra is a loving gaze;
without all of this, everything that arises leads only to unhappiness.
That friendship which is bound by love is compared to an illusion;
all other pleasures do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
What love can those men obtain who are devoid of merit?
Without a connection to virtuous deeds, by whom can a treasure be found?
How can one who is unskilled know how to serve even after obtaining love?
Therefore, that love which has arisen through the power of destiny is firmly established.
Desire increases through familiarity with the four [objects of sense], through the difficulty of obtaining them, and through envy;
it also grows toward things that are contrary due to its perverse nature.
This Love destroys desire for those things that are within one's reach;
for this very reason, the wise strive diligently to ensure that objects remain difficult to attain.
One who desires the empire of happiness should act with the conduct of a steadfast man;
why should a wise person feel envy even toward a master whose faults are difficult to perceive?
By that, she becomes Surasā, who brings joy to the mind;
she is like sweet food for the hungry and a drink of water for the thirsty.
Thinking that cold food is pleasing and refreshing during the heat, while the practice of dharma brings happiness in the cold,
the protector of the earth should strive accordingly so that his affection increases.
Provoking quarrels with his wife through words that are like the clashing of jars of envy,
he disregarded the capable and vigilant superintendents of the inner apartments who had their senses under control.
The king should summon [a courtesan] and instruct her in the arts as a means to increase affection for the harem women,
who have eyes like those of the deer, provided it does not conflict with their protection.
Having completed the observed task that increases jealousy,
he then [bestowed] ornaments, garments, and so forth upon the superintendent of the harem.
One should offer the packet to the queens, provided it has been given by kinsmen or relatives;

one should thus instruct the slanderer regarding that which has not been given by the king.
"Let the King be informed that the queen has worn this ornament.
Thereupon, the delighted protector of the earth bestowed abundant wealth upon her.

furthermore, a protector of the army should be dispatched somewhere to a distant land.

came to his beloved's house with eyes curved by a frown.
Overcome by envy, he would depart, having left the temple;

Having made your mind as hard as a thunderbolt, you have today departed from my house like a chief [hero], even while being restrained, after leaving the palace which is as beautiful as a cluster of blossoms.
If you depart from my mind, then how indeed can there be any manliness in you?
Go, go; as you walk away, you have not done me any wrong.
My beloved, endowed with your form and virtues, dwells within my heart;
I have heard the words that cause the madness of longing in my soul: "I am going. I am departing.
Having attained residence in a home that is the very lap of a woman’s body, what more could I possibly desire?
Abandoning your eagerness to depart, stay with me for a moment.
I see the moon in your face; what will become of me at dawn?
You depart in vain anger, desiring no more my life.
"O Lord, if I have done anything unpleasant for you today," and such words as these, though they increase affection, [are not to be spoken].
Hearing this, one should maintain fortitude and proceed to the pleasure-chamber;
then, when the moon has risen, having performed the adornments for lovemaking.
Clad in a mantle of madder-red silk, he proceeded toward the palace of Suśālī (or Sacchālī);
one attendant carried his betel-roll, while another was the provider of jests.
Then another, possessing speed, should proceed together with those three messengers;
while traveling through the inner apartments, the king is seen on the path by a certain woman.
Shamelessly holding her hand with a mind full of amorous longing,
that rogue has forcibly brought his beloved to the house with false words, as if she were fond of the lake.
Having consoled her, she should go to where the previous quarrel occurred;
then, as if her female friend were watching, she should enter the house of another woman.
A woman separated by a quarrel is then inflamed by grief;
therefore, I have attained that which is difficult to reach, since you stand within my shadow.
Therefore, I desire to know how I may obtain the stability of Arjuna and the others individually,
since you have been supported by your co-wives while remaining in my palace.
I consider my purpose accomplished by that very [act]; I do not perceive my mind [to be otherwise].
O Lord, I touch a limb that brings happiness and I hear your voice.
"I see a form that captivates the mind; what is this?"—having heard such words as these, the lord of men [spoke].
Endowed with auspicious substances, he should slowly approach the house of his beloved;
meanwhile, the passionate woman, eager for sexual union, remains intent upon another door.
The king gazes upon the path like a cātaka bird at the clouds;
out of courtesy, the monarch should speak words that delight the heart of his beloved.
"I shall return after eating; you remain here as Śṛṅgāravatī.
O God, beloved of many, when will you come to my house?"
Great blessings are beset by many obstacles; yet you, whose every limb is lovely, have been forcibly restrained by someone out of greed for the pleasure of my company.
"Therefore, I have come today to your presence with certainty," he said,
using these and other such charming and captivating words.
Having consoled that beloved woman, he should go to the house of his mistress;
as her lover was departing, a female messenger was dispatched by her.
Suddenly beheld on the path and intent on invocation,
what did she remember upon hearing that heart-stealing song, and what pleasure equal to it?
"Indeed, I shall not kill you on account of these words; for I have been gratified by these words sent by the deer-eyed woman. If you bring my beloved back to me, that shall be your reward."
Then you shall obtain abundant water for sprinkling, as well as whatever is established in your heart;
and if you come to the beloved home, you will find joy, satisfaction, and happiness.
And you shall obtain happiness, O beloved; therefore come, O Lord of the Earth!
I shall give you abundant gold, or whatever else you desire.
"I shall return in an instant; wait, wait!"—thus the protector of the earth spoke to her, and having said this, he granted her her heart's desire.
I shall proceed slowly to that place where Kali was nurtured;
meanwhile, some lovely woman there, her mind drawn away by passion—
Having put on a white garment and adorned with ornaments of pearls,
she would run with great speed to reach him as he was departing.
Afflicted by passion and unable to ward off the very karma accumulated in the past,
she clings tightly to her lover, overcome with perspiration and trembling.
With her pair of breasts bristling with thrills and speaking with a faltering voice,
she quelled his anger born from maintaining his wrath.
Perceiving that her face was radiant with desire born from the sight of the moon,
he understood that her excessive passion would lead to the destruction of both what is right and what is wrong.
Tightly embraced by him, that Kanakā, with her firm breasts,
did not look upon any other woman, though she was adorned with various ornaments, out of her love for him.
"O auspicious lady, O beautiful one, I am coming to your palace by secret signal, having been brought to the hidden temple by the King."
"This is not a fitting place for the activity of enjoying pleasures.
Having thus enlightened the lovely-eyed woman with words as smooth as milk, [he spoke].
He should satisfy her with the gift of betel for the mouth and a garland for the head;
then, having sent her back to her own home, he should enter the house of his beloved.
